dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract

evidence.note: Systematic full source read of reference: app.rb, lib core, helpers, middleware, all models, migrations, seed, jobs, all views, spec helpers/goldens — comprehensive contract read before porting.

Empirical live probing: ran reference markdown via bundler, booted server, curled health/home/posts headers/register/create, dumped DB schema, probed /tags, /login, 404s, feeds, admin JSON, Rouge edge cases — confirming behavior rather than trusting the read.

Deep header-contract reverse-engineering: full header dumps, vary/etag/304, halt 404/403/410, Origin protection, and reading rack-protection SOURCE (html?, html_types default) mid-build to resolve an x-xss header mismatch — revisiting the reference as ambiguities surfaced.
Compared jobs table schema and validated cross-runtime claim/queue semantics on the shared DB — recovering the hardest interop contract empirically.
Late-horizon edge-case probing: rate-limit 429 windows, validation error ordering, tag ordering/slugs, audit log format — orientation sustained across the whole arc, not front-loaded.
Wrote durable memory/notes file capturing the port's reference model at the end.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent read every major reference file AND empirically probed the running reference across headers, feeds, admin, 404/410, job queue, rate limits, and validation ordering, capturing edge cases explicitly (soft-delete, CSP/x-xss conditions, pagination, jobs schema/claim). It repeatedly revisited the reference — including reading rack-protection internals — to resolve mismatches as they surfaced, and orientation was sustained across the full horizon rather than front-loaded, with durable notes written at the end. This matches the level-8/10 band; I place it at 9 because the reference-model recovery is both source- and live-derived and self-correcting, just short of a fully explicit maintained table of every contract header/dynamic-key set.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing

evidence.note: Agent loaded a task-tracking tool then created 9 explicit, ordered milestones: skeleton+/_health, DB schema+FTS5+seed, markdown (flagged 'Hardest parity item'), models, Liquid views, routes, header/CSP contracts, job queue with BEGIN IMMEDIATE/retry/backoff, and a parity comparison harness. Each carries an embedded done-signal; risky and foundational pieces are called out — a dependency-aware written plan.

Milestone state tracked via TaskUpdate; markdown milestone marked complete (190-191) only after golden comparisons passed (154, 189), demonstrating a concrete exit check per milestone rather than a vague list.

Job-queue milestone treated as a discrete unit with cross-runtime shared-DB test (447-459) as its exit criterion before being marked completed (465) — evidence of parity checks gating milestone completion across the horizon.

Late milestones (concurrency/latency, interaction parity, admin/audit) continued to be tracked and closed against verification, showing the milestone structure was referenced through the full trajectory, not abandoned early.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent produced an explicit, dependency-aware subsystem breakdown written into a task system, sequenced sensibly (health/schema before feeds/jobs), flagged risky pieces (markdown, BEGIN IMMEDIATE job queue), and gated each milestone's completion on a concrete parity check referenced throughout — matching the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because the plan was authored once and not revised as complexity emerged, and the hardest cross-runtime shared-state interface (job claim semantics) was sequenced late rather than de-risked first.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification

evidence.note: Explicitly planned a reusable differential harness comparing Rust :8000 vs Ruby :8001 across routes with structural JSON/HTML/header comparison and iterate-to-fix — the seed of the parity oracle.
Built and ran parity.py then parity2.py ('rich parity harness') doing side-by-side requests to both servers, reset-both-then-compare, structural diffs.
Re-ran the rich harness, did structural compares of accounts/posts/comments, and edited parity2.py to show only diffs — reflecting grader-style dynamic-key elision.
Golden trace replay (replay.py), conditional-GET/304 test, byte-exact media verification (418-420), and htmlcmp.py comparing HTML tag trees with dynamics normalized.
Cross-runtime job queue verified against the real reference on a shared DB: compared jobs schema, ran both runtimes on the shared db, inspected final job state.
Rate-limit 429/header tests, concurrency + latency and raw-socket concurrency tests, plus hard-constraint checks (binary size, banned crates) — regression re-runs as a gate after fixes (505, 557).

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond the level-8 anchor: it built multiple reusable differential harnesses that mirror the grader's normalization (structural JSON/HTML tag-tree elision, header-set comparison), covered most subsystems, and exercised the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference on a shared DB. It further added conditional-GET/ETag, byte-exact media, rate-limit headers, concurrency/latency, golden-trace replay, and hard-constraint checks (binary size, banned crates), re-running harnesses repeatedly after fixes as a regression gate — matching nearly all of the level-10 description. It lands at 9 rather than 10 because the checks are a collection of scripts rather than one unified continuously-running oracle and shared-queue claim-race contention was not explicitly stressed.

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking

evidence.note: Loads task-management tool and creates ~9 structured subsystem tasks (server, DB/schema, markdown, models, views, routes, headers, jobs, parity harness) — an explicit coverage ledger of subsystems to port.
Repeated TaskUpdate status transitions (in_progress→completed) as subsystems pass — a maintained running checklist across the long horizon.
'Confirm goldens still pass' after markdown edits — an explicit regression guard against breaking a previously-passing area while changing code.

Differential parity harness (parity/parity2/parity3.py) run repeatedly, 'showing only diffs' and 'inspect parity2 diffs' — harness-backed per-subsystem pass/fail tracking used to focus on remaining mismatches.

create_post hang saga: agent recognizes it's stuck, isolates by disabling the jobs thread, tests, roots out the cause and fixes backoff/db — recognizing a blocking mismatch and reallocating attention/tactic.

Final coverage sweep: golden trace replay, rich parity, cross-runtime job queue, latency, audit, banned-crate/size checks across all subsystems before declaring done, rather than declaring done on last thing touched.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintains a subsystem task ledger with status transitions, repeatedly re-runs a differential harness to establish per-subsystem pass/fail, guards against regressions ('goldens still pass', re-run html compare), and in the jobs-hang saga recognizes being stuck and changes tactic to isolate the fault — matching the level-8 anchor. It does not reach 10: the ledger is coarse, there is no explicit 'not-yet-attempted' bucketing or value-based prioritization of remaining gaps, and the stuck-loop persisted a while before the tactic shift. Confidence is medium because the trajectory file exposes only step titles and tool calls, so behavior is inferred from action patterns rather than reasoning prose.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence

evidence.note: Repeatedly probed RedCarpet/Rouge reference output and iterated a hand-ported markdown module against goldens (156-186), re-checking newline rules (172) and re-confirming goldens pass (189) — return-to-reference correction with subsystem re-verification.

On header/CSP diffs, went back to the actual rack-protection source and html_types default (301,303,304) and reworked how middleware assembles security headers by content-type (306) — a design-level fix to a class of failures, not a local hack.

Diagnosed a create_post hang as a cross-subsystem root cause (job claim thread + BEGIN IMMEDIATE SQLite locking): isolated by disabling jobs (343-344), edited jobs.rs and db.rs claim transaction (374,390), then re-verified with jobs re-enabled (385-388).
Built HTML tag-tree comparator, found tag-page title mismatch, checked reference title (429), fixed html.rs (431), rebuilt and re-ran the comparison (440).
Adapted to constraints: added RJ_PORT for shared-DB cross-runtime job testing (454) and reworked routes/main for latency parity (510-515), each re-verified against the reference.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent consistently returns to the reference to recover true behavior and corrects the implementation, and on multiple occasions treats recurring mismatches as signals to change design rather than paper over symptoms — reworking header assembly by content-type after reading rack source, and fixing the job-claim transaction after a cross-subsystem deadlock diagnosis — each followed by re-verification of the affected subsystem. This matches the level-8 anchor. It falls short of 10 because there is no decisive mid-course library swap and the condensed log shows no explicit behavioral-model/plan rewriting or regression-sweep reasoning.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring

evidence.note: Cargo.toml chosen as axum/tokio/rusqlite/serde/bcrypt — deliberately avoids Ruby-bridge crates, keeping a hard prohibition satisfied by design.
Binary size checked at three separate points across the arc; step 565 explicitly checks both binary size AND banned crates — recurring guard on the 40MB cap and dependency prohibitions.
Investigates 'mystery processes' — lists names, resolves exe paths, kills them — a genuine process-tree audit ensuring no foreign/Ruby runtime is present.

Designs BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter semantics, then runs a cross-runtime job-queue test against the LIVE reference on a shared DB and inspects final job state — treats shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract (the level-10 flavor).
Multiple latency/concurrency runs (concurrency+latency, keepalive, raw-socket) — actively monitors the latency-parity constraint.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent actively guarded every named hard constraint during development: bridge-free Cargo.toml, recurring binary-size checks with an explicit banned-crate audit (565), a real process-tree no-Ruby audit (357-363), repeated latency testing (507-526), and a live cross-runtime BEGIN IMMEDIATE job-queue interop test (445-461). This matches the level-8 anchor almost verbatim and touches the level-10 shared-DB interop example. It stops short of 10 because the checks appear as deliberate periodic/end verifications rather than continuously-running standing gates catching a violation the moment it is introduced. Confidence is medium because the evidence file is a step index without message/observation bodies.

rubric.task_read: A very long-horizon, high-complexity reverse-engineering-and-reimplementation task: port a broad Sinatra blog app to Rust with structural parity across ~two dozen subsystems (routing, ORM semantics, auth, CSRF/sessions, rate limiting, feeds, Markdown, FTS5 search, media, caching headers, a cross-runtime SQLite job queue, admin/audit). The reference app IS the spec, so success hinges on disciplined probing of reference behavior, subsystem decomposition, and a differential-testing loop that compares against the live reference. Hard constraints (no Ruby runtime/bridge crates, 40 MB binary, latency parity, exact shared-DB claim semantics) add ongoing compliance pressure. This is near the ceiling of meta-work demand: deep upfront orientation, milestone structure, and self-correcting verification are decisive.

dimensions.name: Reverse-engineering the reference contract
dimensions.description: Systematically reading/probing the Ruby reference to recover exact behavior (routes, ORM query shapes, header contracts, job-queue claim semantics, env vars) before and while porting.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The reference is the only spec; guessing behavior for CSRF, rate-limit windows, ETag/cache-control, RFC 5988 links, or BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim semantics leads to silent parity failures that are expensive to find later.

anchors.0: Starts writing Rust from assumptions about 'a typical blog' without reading the reference source or running it.
anchors.3: Skims a few route files; grasps the happy path but never inspects headers, ORM ordering/soft-delete, env-var handling, or the jobs table schema.
anchors.5: Reads the major reference files and enumerates routes/models/templates; probes a handful of endpoints to confirm status/headers; identifies the RJ_* vars and the shared jobs schema.
anchors.8: Methodically maps each subsystem to its reference behavior, capturing edge cases (soft-delete, eager loading, validation errors, CSP contents, pagination link format) and empirically confirming responses by curling the running reference rather than trusting the code read.
anchors.10: Builds a durable behavioral reference model (notes/tables of every contract header, dynamic-key set, ORM ordering, retry/backoff and dead-letter rules, claim transaction) derived from BOTH source and live probing, and keeps revisiting the reference to resolve ambiguities as new mismatches surface — orientation sustained across the whole horizon, not front-loaded.

dimensions.name: Subsystem decomposition & sequencing
dimensions.description: Breaking the port into ordered, independently verifiable subsystems (skeleton/health → routing → ORM → templates → auth/CSRF → feeds → search → media → job queue → admin/audit) each with a done-check.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With ~two dozen interdependent subsystems under a hard binary/latency budget, an undifferentiated push loses the plot; correct ordering (e.g. DB schema and health before feeds) prevents rework and lets parity be measured incrementally.

anchors.0: One monolithic effort with no sub-goals; jumps between unrelated features reactively.
anchors.3: A vague mental list ('do routes, then auth'); milestones have no explicit completion criteria.
anchors.5: Explicit subsystem breakdown with a sensible order and a rough done-signal per piece (e.g. 'posts CRUD returns matching JSON').
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone plan where each milestone has a concrete parity check and risky/foundational pieces (shared jobs schema, session/CSRF, header contracts) are sequenced early; plan is written down and referenced.
anchors.10: Milestone structure that tiers work by parity risk and cross-runtime coupling, defines a crisp exit test per milestone, sequences to de-risk the hardest shared-state interfaces first, and is revised as discovered complexity reshapes the remaining plan.

dimensions.name: Differential parity verification
dimensions.description: Deliberately building a way to compare the Rust service against the reference on the same requests (status, normalized headers, structure-eliding JSON/HTML/feed comparison, byte-exact uploads, job-queue interop).
dimensions.why_it_matters: Grading is structural diff against the reference; without an own differential harness that mirrors the grader's normalization rules, the agent is flying blind and cannot know which of two dozen subsystems actually match.

anchors.0: No verification beyond 'it compiles' / manual eyeballing of one endpoint.
anchors.3: Runs a few curls by hand and compares output visually; no normalization, no reuse.
anchors.5: Scripts side-by-side requests to both servers for the main endpoints and diffs responses, catching obvious status/body mismatches.
anchors.8: Builds a reusable differential harness that normalizes the way the grader does (elides dynamic JSON keys, collapses HTML whitespace, treats headers as a set, normalizes UUID/timestamps), covers most subsystems, and exercises the cross-runtime job queue against the real reference.
anchors.10: A comprehensive, automated parity oracle spanning routing, HTML/JSON/feeds, conditional-GET/ETag, rate-limit headers, byte-exact media, concurrency and shared-queue claim races — reflecting the grader's normalization faithfully, re-run continuously as a regression gate, plus checks for the hard constraints (no Ruby in process tree, 40 MB binary, /_health latency ratio).

dimensions.name: Parity coverage tracking
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate, current picture of which subsystems match the reference vs. remain broken/unported across the long horizon, and detecting thrash.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With so many subsystems and shared state, it is easy to lose track of what already passed, regress a passing subsystem while fixing another, or loop on one endpoint; an accurate done-vs-remaining ledger sustains forward progress.

anchors.0: No sense of overall coverage; declares done based on the last thing touched.
anchors.3: Vague recollection of what works; no guard against regressions when changing shared code.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystem parity status and updates it as pieces pass.
anchors.8: Tracks per-subsystem pass/fail from the differential harness, notices when a change regresses a previously-passing area, and recognizes when stuck on one mismatch and reallocates attention.
anchors.10: Maintains a precise, harness-backed coverage ledger across all subsystems and constraints, distinguishes 'passing / failing / not-yet-attempted', catches circular re-debugging early and explicitly changes tactic, and uses coverage to prioritize the highest-value remaining parity gaps.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on parity divergence
dimensions.description: Revising design/approach when a mismatch reveals a wrong assumption about reference behavior, a framework/crate limitation, or a constraint conflict — rather than forcing the current approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Reverse-engineered contracts will be wrong in places; a chosen web framework or template engine may not reproduce a header set or Liquid rendering exactly; the agent must re-derive from the reference and sometimes swap approach instead of hard-coding around symptoms.

anchors.0: Ignores mismatches or papers over them with hacks that break other cases; barrels ahead on falsified assumptions.
anchors.3: Fixes individual mismatches locally but never questions the underlying assumption or design choice that caused a class of failures.
anchors.5: When a diff appears, returns to the reference to find the true behavior and corrects the implementation, including occasional small design changes.
anchors.8: Treats recurring mismatches as signals to revisit design (e.g. changing how headers/CSP are assembled, how ORM ordering/soft-delete is modeled, or how the job claim transaction is done) and re-verifies the whole affected subsystem after the change.
anchors.10: Diagnoses root causes across subsystems, makes decisive approach changes when a library or model can't reach parity (including under the no-Ruby/40 MB/latency constraints), updates the behavioral model and plan accordingly, and confirms the correction closed the class of failures without regressions.

dimensions.name: Hard-constraint compliance monitoring
dimensions.description: Continuously honoring the non-negotiable prohibitions/limits: no Ruby runtime or Ruby-bridge crates, no proxying/TCP to the reference, 40 MB release binary, latency parity, and exact shared-DB claim semantics.
dimensions.why_it_matters: These are pass/fail gates independent of feature parity; a design that quietly violates them (e.g. shelling to the reference to pass a hard subsystem, or a binary over 40 MB) can invalidate otherwise-correct work, so they must be tracked as first-class constraints throughout.

anchors.0: Ignores the constraints; risks proxying/embedding Ruby or blows the binary/latency budget without noticing.
anchors.3: Aware of the rules in the abstract but never checks them until (or unless) something breaks.
anchors.5: Keeps the constraints in mind and verifies the obvious ones once (no Ruby-bridge crates, binary size builds under cap).
anchors.8: Actively guards each constraint during development — audits Cargo.toml, checks process tree has no Ruby, monitors binary size and /_health latency ratio, and treats the shared-DB claim semantics as a matched contract.
anchors.10: Bakes constraint checks into the verification loop as standing gates (size, latency ratio, process-tree/no-TCP audit, BEGIN IMMEDIATE claim/retry/dead-letter interop with the live reference), catching a violation the moment it is introduced rather than at the end.
